Speaker
SPEE-ker
n. (one who speaks; a spokesman)
Old English sprecan, to speak. The noun occurs twice in the Authorized Version, and the two uses are a study in contrast: an evil speaker the psalmist asks God to unseat, and the chief speaker whom a pagan city mistook for a god.

Biblical Definition

David prays against a man defined by his mouth: “Let not an evil speaker be established in the earth: evil shall hunt the violent man to overthrow him” (Psalm 140:11). The petition is that such a man should not be established — not merely that he be silenced, but that he never acquire a settled place from which to speak. The New Testament use is at Lystra, where a healing brought the crowd out with garlands: “And they called Barnabas, Jupiter; and Paul, Mercurius, because he was the chief speaker” (Acts 14:12). Facility with words drew the divine honour, and Paul's response was to rend his clothes and run in among them crying that they were men of like passions. The two verses set the biblical estimate of the gifted tongue: it is a real power, capable of establishing a man or of getting him worshipped, and it is therefore the faculty most in need of a governor.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a speaker as one who speaks; one who utters or pronounces a discourse; and the presiding officer of a deliberative assembly.

expand to see more

SPEAKER, n. One that speaks, in whatever manner. One who utters or pronounces a discourse; usually, one who utters a speech in public.

SPEAKER, n. The presiding officer of a legislative body, so called because he speaks or promulgates the will of the house.

SPOKESMAN, n. One who speaks for another; one who is deputed to speak in the name of another.

ELOQUENCE, n. The act or art of speaking well; oratory; the power of expressing strong emotions in striking language.

SLANDER, n. A false tale or report maliciously uttered, tending to injure the reputation of another.

Key Scripture

Psalm 140:11 — "Let not an evil speaker be established in the earth: evil shall hunt the violent man to overthrow him."

Acts 14:12 — "And they called Barnabas, Jupiter; and Paul, Mercurius, because he was the chief speaker."

Acts 14:15 — "And saying, Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God, which made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are therein:"

James 3:5 — "Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!"

Modern Corruption

The culture measures a speaker by reach and effect, so that a man who can hold a crowd is credited with authority; Scripture treats the same facility as a power to be feared, and asks that the evil speaker never be established.

expand to see more

Platforms are now awarded for the ability to command attention, and the church has borrowed the standard. A man who speaks well is assumed to have something worth saying, and a hearing is granted on the strength of the delivery. Lystra made exactly that mistake in its purest form: Paul was the chief speaker, therefore Paul was Mercurius, and the oxen and garlands were already at the gates. Paul's reaction is the model — he rent his clothes, he denied the honour, he insisted he was a man of like passions, and he turned the crowd from vanities to the living God.

Psalm 140:11 asks something sharper still: that the evil speaker not be established in the earth. It is a prayer against permanence — against the slanderer acquiring an institution, a following, a settled seat. James says the tongue is a little member that boasteth great things, and Scripture never treats speech as merely expressive. It builds and it burns. The recovery is to weigh speakers by the truth of what they say and the holiness of how they live, and to pray that God would refuse a lasting foothold to the men whose gift is only their mouth.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ish lashon, a man of tongue; kun (H3559), to establish; Greek logos (G3056), word or speech; hegeomai (G2233), to lead, hence chief.

expand to see more

Hebrew ish lashon — literally a man of tongue; the evil speaker of Psalm 140:11.

Hebrew kun (H3559) — to set up, establish, make firm; what David asks God to withhold.

Greek logos (G3056) — word, speech, discourse; the substance a speaker is judged by.

Greek hegeomai (G2233) — to lead the way; behind the phrase the chief speaker at Lystra.

Greek glossa (G1100) — the tongue; a little member that boasteth great things.

Usage

"“Let not an evil speaker be established in the earth” — a prayer against permanence."

"“Because he was the chief speaker” — and they brought oxen and garlands."

"“We also are men of like passions with you” — the apostolic refusal."
